title: Medicare's Fraud Prevention System helps identify or prevent $654.8 million in inappropriate payments in 2015
summary: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services count $654.8 million in inappropriate Medicare payments identified or prevented in 2015 with help from their Fraud Prevention System.
account: The report “Fraud Prevention System Return on Investment, Fourth Implementation Year” of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is undated. The Wayback Machine archived it on 24 August 2016. It states that the Fraud Prevention System (FPS) helped identify or prevent $654.8 million in inappropriate payments during calendar year 2015, about 44% more than the previous year. That total counts actions taken due to the FPS and investigations that it expedited, augmented or corroborated. The report gives a corrected return on investment of $11.5 to $1. The originally reported $11.6 contained a rounding error. Table 1 shows identified savings of $115.4 million in the first year (July 2011 to June 2012), $250.1 million in the second and $454.0 million in the third. The cumulative total is $1,474.3 million. The savings come from claims denied by pre-payment edits, payment suspensions, projected cost avoidance from revoking billing privileges and overpayments referred for recovery. The value of referrals to law enforcement was $49.2 million in 2015. The report says that the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services certified the methodology. It counts 45 providers on active payment suspension at year end. Costs were an estimated $57.1 million. They include $19.5 million for a developing contractor and $4.8 million for a modeling contractor. The report does not describe the system's technique. In a report of 30 August 2017, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that FPS leads started about 20 percent of contractor fraud investigations in fiscal 2015 and 2016. GAO found that these investigations led to corrective actions and savings. Contractor officials told GAO that FPS generally did not speed up investigations once they began. GAO notes that CMS estimated actual savings of $133 million for 2014 against $454 million identified. CMS reported to GAO that FPS edits denied nearly 169,000 claims and saved $11.3 million in fiscal 2015. In fiscal 2016 the edits denied nearly 324,000 claims and saved $20.4 million. CMS had 24 prepayment edits in place by May 2017.
purpose: The system is meant to identify or prevent inappropriate Medicare payments by generating leads that program-integrity contractors investigate and act on.
developer: Contractors engaged by CMS (the report lists 'Developing Contractor Costs' and 'Modeling Contractor Costs' without naming firms)
deployer: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
domain: Health insurance fraud and improper payments

ratings.reason: The Medicare program saved money through denied claims, payment suspensions and referred overpayments. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services count $654.8 million identified or prevented in 2015. They reported to the Government Accountability Office that the system's edits denied nearly 169,000 claims and saved $11.3 million in fiscal 2015. These are cost savings for the Medicare program.
Savings to the Medicare program are stated only as yearly totals that mix denied claims with projected avoidance, and no source traces an effect on beneficiaries or taxpayers.

ai_role.statement: GAO found that FPS leads started about 20 percent of contractor investigations in fiscal 2015 and 2016. Contractor officials told GAO that FPS sped up the finding and triage of suspect providers, but that it generally did not speed up the investigations themselves. Investigators did the case work, and the FPS prepayment edits apply Medicare rules without scoring risk, so the dollar totals combine model-generated leads, rule-based edits and human investigation.

fields.summary: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services count $654.8 million in inappropriate Medicare payments identified or prevented in 2015 with help from their Fraud Prevention System.
fields.account: The report “Fraud Prevention System Return on Investment, Fourth Implementation Year” of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is undated. The Wayback Machine archived it on 24 August 2016. It states that the Fraud Prevention System (FPS) helped identify or prevent $654.8 million in inappropriate payments during calendar year 2015, about 44% more than the previous year. That total counts actions taken due to the FPS and investigations that it expedited, augmented or corroborated. The report gives a corrected return on investment of $11.5 to $1. The originally reported $11.6 contained a rounding error. Table 1 shows identified savings of $115.4 million in the first year (July 2011 to June 2012), $250.1 million in the second and $454.0 million in the third. The cumulative total is $1,474.3 million. The savings come from claims denied by pre-payment edits, payment suspensions, projected cost avoidance from revoking billing privileges and overpayments referred for recovery. The value of referrals to law enforcement was $49.2 million in 2015. The report says that the Office of Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services certified the methodology. It counts 45 providers on active payment suspension at year end. Costs were an estimated $57.1 million. They include $19.5 million for a developing contractor and $4.8 million for a modeling contractor. The report does not describe the system's technique. In a report of 30 August 2017, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that FPS leads started about 20 percent of contractor fraud investigations in fiscal 2015 and 2016. GAO found that these investigations led to corrective actions and savings. Contractor officials told GAO that FPS generally did not speed up investigations once they began. GAO notes that CMS estimated actual savings of $133 million for 2014 against $454 million identified. CMS reported to GAO that FPS edits denied nearly 169,000 claims and saved $11.3 million in fiscal 2015. In fiscal 2016 the edits denied nearly 324,000 claims and saved $20.4 million. CMS had 24 prepayment edits in place by May 2017.
